Surrender is the only path to survival (verses 1–10)

After the siege began, King Zedekiah sent messengers to ask Jeremiah how the conflict would end.

During danger and distress, people often seek the advice and prayers of those they normally despise and oppose.

Yet often they want only to escape the punishment of their sin, without giving up the sin itself.

Those who profess religion but persist in disobedience must not suppose their outward privileges will protect them.

The Lord may grant success even to open enemies when they are sent in judgment against his disobedient people.

The king and his officials would not surrender, but the prophet urged the people to surrender in order to preserve their lives.

No sinner on earth who truly wants a refuge has been left without one.

But the road of life is humbling.

It requires self-denial and may expose the traveler to real difficulties.

The household of David is urged to practice justice (verses 11–14)

The sin of the king and his family was especially serious because of their connection with David.

They were called to do justice immediately, before the Lord's anger burned beyond restraint.

If God is for us, who can stand against us?

But if God is against us, who can possibly help us?

Royal authority must be exercised justly (verses 1–9)

The king of Judah sat on David's throne, and David had been a man after God's heart.

The king should have followed David's example so that he could share the benefit of the promises made to that family.

The surest way to preserve a government is for its rulers to perform the duties of government.

But sin destroys the households of princes as readily as those of ordinary people.

Who can resist destroyers whom God has appointed?

God destroys neither people, cities nor nations without the cause of sin.

Often even in this life he makes clear the wrongs for which he sends punishment.

At the final judgment, those reasons will be completely evident.

The sons of Josiah reject their father's example (verses 10–19)

The passage announces a sentence of death over two kings, wicked sons of a deeply godly father.

Josiah was spared the sight of the approaching calamity.

He was taken from this life to behold the good of the world to come.

Therefore the people had greater reason to weep for Shallum, who would live and die as a miserable captive, than for their father.

The death of a faithful believer may be cause for hope, while the continued life of an unrepentant person may rightly call forth pity.

The prophecy also announces the fate of Jehoiakim.

It is lawful for rulers and great people to build, improve and furnish their houses.

But those who make their homes grander must guard against vanity and pride.

Jehoiakim built through injustice.

His money had been acquired wrongfully, and he refused to pay his workers their wages.

God sees the wrong powerful people do to servants and laborers, and will repay in justice those who have refused to pay others what justice demands.

Even the most powerful person must regard the poorest person as a neighbor owed fairness.

Jehoiakim also shed innocent blood.

Greed, the root of every kind of evil, lay beneath his wickedness.

Children who dismiss the old ways of their parents often miss the true excellence beneath those customs.

Jehoiakim knew his father had found obedience to be a path of comfort, yet refused to follow him.

He would die without mourning, having become hated for oppression and cruelty.

The royal family's confidence collapses (verses 20–30)

Judah's condition had three distinct stages.

First, the people were arrogant during peace and security.

Then they became fearful when trouble was announced.

Finally, they were utterly crushed under the weight of disaster.

Many people feel no real shame over sin until it has brought them into the most desperate circumstances.

The king would end his days in captivity.

Those imagining themselves to be like signet rings upon God's right hand should not presume they can never be removed.

The king and his family would be transported to Babylon.

We know where we were born, but we do not know where we will die.

God knows both.

Our responsibility is to make sure that we die in Christ.

Then it will be well with us wherever death comes, even far from home.

The king who had once been admired would become despised.

People in whom God takes no pleasure may eventually become a disappointment to everyone else too.

If someone has no children, God has permitted that condition; a person who spends the available years without doing good cannot expect to prosper.

How little we should depend on royal splendor or flourishing families!

But those who hear Christ's voice and follow him possess eternal life.

They will never perish, and no enemy can tear them from his almighty hands.

God destroys neither persons, cities, nor nations, except for sin; even in this world he often makes it plain for what crimes he sends punishment; and it will be clear at the day of judgement.
[Jer.22.10-Jer.22.19]
Verses 10-19 Here is a sentence of death upon two kings, the wicked sons of a very pious father. Josiah was prevented from seeing the evil to come in this world, and removed to see the good to come in the other world; therefore, weep not for him, but for his son Shallum, who is likely to live and die a wretched captive. Dying saints may be justly envied, while living sinners are justly pitied. Here also is the doom of Jehoiakim. No doubt it is lawful for princes and great men to build, beautify, and furnish houses; but those who enlarge their houses, and make them sumptuous, need carefully to watch against the workings of vain-glory. He built his houses by unrighteousness, with money gotten unjustly. And he defrauded his workmen of their wages. God notices the wrong done by the greatest to poor servants and labourers, and will repay those in justice, who will not, in justice, pay those whom they employ. The greatest of men must look upon the meanest as their neighbours, and be just to them accordingly. Jehoiakim was unjust, and made no conscience of shedding innocent blood. Covetousness, which is the root of all evil, was at the bottom of all. The children who despise their parents' old fashions, commonly come short of their real excellences. Jehoiakim knew that his father found the way of duty to be the way of comfort, yet he would not tread in his steps. He shall die unlamented, hateful for oppression and cruelty.
[Jer.22.20-Jer.22.30]
Verses 20-30 The Jewish state is described under a threefold character. Very haughty in a day of peace and safety. Very fearful on alarm of trouble. Very much cast down under pressure of trouble. Many never are ashamed of their sins till brought by them to the last extremity. The king shall close his days in bondage. Those that think themselves as signets on God's right hand, must not be secure, but fear lest they should be plucked thence. The Jewish king and his family shall be carried to Babylon. We know where we were born, but where we shall die we know not; it is enough that our God knows. Let it be our care that we die in Christ, then it will be well with us wherever we die, thought it may be in a far country. The Jewish king shall be despised. Time was when he was delighted in; but all those in whom God has no pleasure, some time or other, will be so lowered, that men will have no pleasure in them. Whoever are childless, it is the Lord that writes them so; and those who take no care to do good in their days, cannot expect to prosper. How little is earthly grandeur to be depended upon, or flourishing families to be rejoiced in! But those who hear the voice of Christ, and follow him, have eternal life, and shall never perish, neither shall any enemy pluck them out of his almighty hands.

Christ, the righteous Branch and faithful Shepherd (verses 1–8)

Woe to people appointed to feed God's flock who refuse to care about the sheep's welfare!

Yet the neglected flock receives a promise of comfort.

Even if only a remnant remains, God will find his scattered sheep and bring them home.

Jesus Christ is the Branch from David's family.

He is righteous himself, and through him all his people become righteous.

He breaks Satan's illegitimate power.

The spiritual descendants of believing Abraham and praying Jacob will be rescued from the guilt and dominion of sin.

When Christ rules within a human soul, that soul lives in safety.

His name is “The LORD Our Righteousness.”

He is our righteousness in a way no created being could ever be.

His obedience unto death is the righteousness that justifies believers and gives them the right to heavenly happiness.

Our sanctification, which becomes the source of our own obedience, comes from our union with Christ and the Holy Spirit he supplies.

Every genuine believer can call upon Christ by this precious name.

We have nothing to plead except that Christ died and rose again, and that we have received him as our Lord.

The righteousness he achieved to satisfy God's law and justice is freely given to us.

Through the Holy Spirit, we are clothed in that righteousness, enabled to take hold of it and assured of our share in it.

“The LORD Our Righteousness” is a wonderfully comforting name for someone convicted of sin, conscious of guilt and aware of the need for a righteousness not their own.

This salvation surpasses every former rescue God gave his church.

May we be gathered to Christ and found in him.

False prophets make people confident in sin (verses 9–22)

The false prophets of Samaria misled Israel into idolatry.

But the Lord judged the prophets of Jerusalem to have practiced even worse wickedness, making others bold in sin.

These teachers would suffer bitter judgment.

They first persuaded themselves that wrongdoing was harmless and acted on that belief.

Then they persuaded others to accept it.

People determined to persist in evil may be given over to strong delusions.

What divine revelation had these teachers actually received?

What had they understood of God's word?

Eventually they would look back on their folly and unbelief with remorse.

True prophets' instruction and conduct lead people toward repentance, faith and righteousness.

False prophets encourage people to rest in religious forms and opinions while remaining undisturbed in sin.

Let us be careful not to follow unrighteousness.

False dreams are not God's word (verses 23–32)

No one can hide from the God who sees everything.

Why do false prophets fail to see the judgment their words are bringing upon themselves?

Consider the vast difference between their utterances and the prophecies of God's true messengers.

Their dreams must not be described as divine revelations.

Promises of peace invented by those teachers compare to God's promises as chaff compares to wheat.

The heart of a person who has not been humbled resembles a rock.

If the word of God does not melt it like fire, the word may break it like a hammer.

Who could remain safe or peaceful with almighty God against them?

His word is not a smooth, soothing or deceitful message intended to lull sinners to sleep.

Its faithfulness to truth distinguishes it from false doctrine.

Mocking prophecy cannot cancel judgment (verses 33–40)

How miserable are people forsaken and forgotten by God!

Mocking the Lord's judgments does not make them fail.

God had once taken Israel as a people close to himself.

Now they would be cast out of his presence.

It is a sign of extreme irreverence to treat God's own words as a joke.

Every idle and profane word increases the guilt sinners must answer for at judgment.

If they remain unrepentant, everlasting disgrace awaits them.

Original source heading

Good and bad figs represent the Jews in captivity, and those who remain in their own land.

Two baskets of figs

Jeremiah saw two baskets of figs set before the temple as first-fruit offerings.

The figs in one basket were very good.

Those in the other were very bad.

What creature is more degraded than someone who persists in wickedness?

And who is more valuable than a truly godly person?

This vision was intended to encourage those already in exile, assuring them that they would have a happy return.

It also warned and humbled the proud people who remained in Jerusalem, telling them that they would experience miserable captivity.

The good figs represent the faithful captives.

We cannot determine God's love or hatred simply from the outward circumstances before us.

Sometimes early suffering proves to be for the best.

When a child receives correction promptly, the correction may have a better effect.

The exile itself was intended for the people's good.

God's good purposes never fail.

Affliction convinced them of sin, humbled them under his hand, loosened their attachment to the world, taught them to pray and led them away from sin—especially from idolatry.

God promised to acknowledge these people as his own even in captivity.

The Lord recognizes everyone who truly belongs to him, whatever their outward condition.

He promised to protect them during trouble and to bring them to a glorious deliverance at the proper time.

When suffering is sanctified to us, we can trust that it will end for our good.

The people would return to God with their whole hearts.

Then they could once again acknowledge him as their God, pray to him and hope for his blessings.

The bad figs represented Zedekiah and his party who remained in the land.

They would be removed for their harm and become despised among nations.

God possesses many kinds of judgment.

People who escape one may still meet another, until they are brought to repentance.

The prophecy certainly found fulfillment in Jeremiah's time.

But Henry adds that the Spirit of prophecy may also have been looking ahead to the later scattering of unbelieving Jews among the nations.

Those who desire blessing from God should ask him to give them a heart that truly knows him.
classic_reading:
[Jer.24.1]
Chapter 24
Good and bad figs represent the Jews in captivity, and those who remain in their own land.
The prophet saw two baskets of figs set before the temple, as offerings of first-fruits. The figs in one basket were very good, those in the other basket very bad. What creature viler than a wicked man? and what more valuable than a godly man? This vision was to raise the spirits of those gone into captivity, by assuring them of a happy return; and to humble and awaken the proud and secure spirits of those yet in Jerusalem, by assuring them of a miserable captivity. The good figs represents the pious captives. We cannot determine as to God's love or hatred by what is before us. Early suffering sometimes proves for the best. The sooner the child is corrected, the better effect the correction is likely to have. Even this captivity was for their good; and God's intentions never are in vain. By afflictions they were convinced of sin, humbled under the hand of God, weaned from the world, taught to pray, and turned from sins, particularly from idolatry. God promises that he will own them in captivity. The Lord will own those who are his, in all conditions. God assures them of his protection in trouble, and a glorious deliverance in due time. When our troubles are sanctified to us, we may be sure that they will end well. They shall return to him with their whole heart. Thus they should have liberty to own him for their God, to pray to him, and expect blessings from him. The bad figs were Zedekiah and those of his party yet in the land. These should be removed for their hurt, and forsaken of all mankind. God has many judgments, and those that escape one, may expect another, till they are brought to repent. Doubtless, this prophecy had its fulfilment in that age; but the Spirit of prophecy may here look forward to the dispersion of the unbelieving Jews, in all the nations of the earth. Let those who desire blessings from the Lord, beg that he will give them a heart to know him.

Original chapter outlineOriginal outlineVersesThe Jews rebuked for not obeying calls to repentance.1–7Their captivity during seventy years is expressly foretold.8–14Desolations upon the nations shown by the emblem of a cup of wrath.15–29The judgments again declared.30–38
The people reject repeated calls to repent (verses 1–7)

God calls sinners everywhere to abandon their evil ways, return to his worship and service, trust in Christ and share in his salvation.

The Lord takes account of how long we have possessed the means of grace.

The longer we enjoy those opportunities without making good use of them, the heavier our responsibility becomes.

The prophets' practice of rising early to call the people reveals God's earnest desire that sinners turn from their ways and live.

A nation cannot truly be rescued while its inhabitants refuse personal reform.

Every person must turn from their own evil way.

Yet the people would not listen.

They refused the only right way to turn away God's anger.

Seventy years of captivity and the judgment of Babylon (verses 8–14)

God announced exactly how long the Jewish exile would last: seventy years.

That definite period confirmed the prophecy and also comforted believers, encouraging them to pray and trust.

Babylon's ruin was also foretold.

When the instrument God used to correct his people had completed its work, the rod itself would be thrown into the fire.

When the appointed time came to favor Zion, Babylon would be judged for its own sins, just as other nations had been judged.

Every warning in Scripture will be fulfilled.

The nations drink the cup of judgment (verses 15–29)

Scripture often represents life's blessings and calamities as cups.

The cup in this chapter pictures the coming destruction of many nations.

Nebuchadnezzar had just begun his reign and campaigns and would be the instrument.

But the destroying sword would ultimately act under God's authority.

The disorder the sword would bring upon these kingdoms is compared to the effects of excessive drinking.

This comparison should increase our hatred of drunkenness.

It deprives people of reason, can make them behave like mad people, and steals the precious gift of health.

Drunkenness is also a sin that punishes itself.

The image should also teach us to fear war.

War can quickly fill an entire country with confusion.

The nations would refuse to accept Jeremiah's warning.

But he was to tell them that the Lord of Hosts had spoken.

Resistance to almighty power would be useless.

If God's judgment begins with people who have professed faith and then turned away, unrepentant wicked people cannot expect to escape.

God's controversy with all nations (verses 30–38)

The Lord has righteous grounds of complaint against every nation and every human being.

He will judge all the wicked.

Who could avoid trembling when he speaks in displeasure?

The appointed time had arrived—the time fixed in God's own counsel for bringing desolation upon the nations.

Even the gentle and delicate would share the common distress.

People who had lived peaceably and done nothing to provoke war would still suffer its effects.

But blessed be God: there is a peaceful dwelling above for everyone who belongs to the Lord's peace.

He will preserve his church and every believer through all changes, for nothing can separate them from his love.

Rising early, points out the earnest desire that this people should turn and live. Verses 8-14 The fixing of the time during which the Jewish captivity should last, would not only confirm the prophecy, but also comfort the people of God, and encourage faith and prayer. The ruin of Babylon is foretold: the rod will be thrown into the fire when the correcting work is done. Every threatening of the Scripture will certainly be accomplished.
[Jer.25.15-Jer.25.29]
Verses 15-29 The evil and the good events of life are often represented in Scripture as cups. Under this figure is represented the desolation then coming upon that part of the world, of which Nebuchadnezzar, who had just began to reign and act, was to be the instrument; but this destroying sword would come from the hand of God. The desolations the sword should make in all these kingdoms, are represented by the consequences of excessive drinking. This may make us loathe the sin of drunkenness, that the consequences of it are used to set forth such a woful condition. Drunkenness deprives men of the use of their reason, makes men as mad. It takes from them the valuable blessing, health; and is a sin which is its own punishment. This may also make us dread the judgments of war. It soon fills a nation with confusion. They will refuse to take the cup at thy hand. They will not believe Jeremiah; but he must tell them it is the word of the Lord of hosts, and it is in vain for them to struggle against Almighty power. And if God's judgments begin with backsliding professors, let not the wicked expect to escape.
[Jer.25.30-Jer.25.38]

Even those who used to live in peace, and did nothing to provoke, shall not escape. Blessed be God, there is a peaceable habitation above, for all the sons of peace. The Lord will preserve his church and all believers in all changes; for nothing can separate them from his love.

God's messenger must speak without fear (verses 1–6)

People sent to speak on God's behalf must not shape their message to please human beings or merely to protect themselves from harm.

Notice how patiently God waits for an opportunity to show mercy.

If the people continued refusing obedience, Jerusalem and its temple would be ruined.

What else could they expect?

People unwilling to submit to God's commands make themselves subject to his judgment.

Jeremiah is accused and threatened (verses 7–15)

The priests and prophets accused Jeremiah of deserving death and gave false testimony against him.

The leaders of Israel came to investigate.

Jeremiah explained that the Lord had sent him to deliver this warning.

Ministers who remain faithful to the word they have received from God need not be ruled by fear.

It is deeply unjust to blame a minister simply for preaching judgment and condemnation, when the purpose is to lead hearers toward heaven and salvation.

Jeremiah warned the people that killing or injuring him would bring still more guilt upon them.

Anyone who harms, kills or hates a faithful person who corrects wrongdoing hastens and increases their own judgment.

The elders defend the prophet (verses 16–24)

God's word gives sufficient reason to warn secure sinners that continuing in sin may lead to the removal of the Spirit's gracious work and the privileges of God's kingdom.

Consider the contrasting examples.

Hezekiah protected Micah and prospered.

Jehoiakim killed Urijah. Did he prosper?

Evil people's behavior and the consequences of their actions should deter us from following them.

Urijah faithfully proclaimed the message given to him.

But Henry judges that he acted wrongly by abandoning his appointed work.

The Lord permitted Urijah to die, while Jeremiah was protected amid danger.

Those who rely most simply upon the Lord are safest in the truest sense, regardless of outward circumstances.

Knowing that all human hearts are in God's hands encourages believers to trust him while fulfilling their duties.

He will honor and reward those who treat kindly people persecuted for his sake.

A prophet who promises only peace and prosperity, without warning that deliberate sin cuts people off from God's favor, will prove to be a false prophet.

Anyone who refuses to proclaim the alarming as well as the encouraging parts of God's word—and fails to call people to repentance, faith and holiness—follows the pattern of the false prophets.

Christ's gospel encourages people to perform deeds worthy of repentance.

It never gives anyone permission to continue in sin.

Hananiah was sentenced to die.

Jeremiah told him this boldly only after receiving God's direction, not before the Lord had entrusted him with the message.

People who assure sinners that they will enjoy peace while they harden themselves against God's word bear terrible responsibility.

The Lord's servant must be gentle toward everyone.

Live faithfully while waiting in Babylon (verses 1–7)

God's written word is just as truly inspired as his spoken word.

A zealous servant of the Lord will use every means available to help people who are far away as well as nearby.

Writing is especially useful for that purpose.

The invention of printing made it still easier for many people to receive the knowledge of God's word.

The letter showed that God had not abandoned the exiles, even though their disobedience had brought his correction upon them.

If they continued to fear the Lord, they could still live comfortably in Babylon.

In every condition of life, wisdom and duty require us not to abandon the comfort we do possess simply because we lack everything we wish to possess.

The exiles were instructed to seek the welfare of the country where they were held captive.

As long as Babylon's king protected them, they should live quiet, peaceful, godly and honest lives under his authority.

They must wait patiently for God to bring deliverance at his appointed time.

God's good purposes are fulfilled in his time (verses 8–19)

Be careful when choosing which prophets to listen to.

Do not mistake people who share your preferences for prophets sent by God, or your own imaginings and dreams for divine revelations.

False prophets flatter people who enjoy being flattered.

Their hearers speak kindly to them so that the prophets will tell their hearers what they want to hear.

God promised the exiles would return after seventy years.

Henry notes that this period must be counted from the first deportation, not the final one.

The return would fulfill God's good word to them.

God's purposes are firm.

Human beings may not even know what they truly want, but the Lord is never uncertain.

At times we fear that all his plans for us are against us.

Yet for those who belong to him, even what appears evil will ultimately serve their good.

He gives them not the outcomes imagined by their fears, nor the wishes entertained by their fantasies, but the future promised to their faith—which is best for them.

When God pours out a special spirit of prayer, that is a hopeful sign that he is approaching a people in mercy.

His promises are intended to encourage prayer.

He has never told sincere seekers to seek him in vain.

But those who remained in Jerusalem would be destroyed despite the assurances given by false prophets.

The reason repeatedly stated also explains the final ruin of impenitent sinners:

God called them, but they refused to hear his word.

False prophets are judged for their lies (verses 20–32)

Jeremiah announced judgment upon false prophets who had deceived the Jews in Babylon.

Lying is wrong.

Lying to God's people in order to give them false confidence is worse.

But pretending that one's own lies are spoken by the God of truth is worst of all.

These teachers flattered others in their sins because they could not condemn those sins without condemning themselves.

Even hidden wrongdoing is known to God.

A day will come when he brings every concealed work of darkness into the light.

Shemaiah urged the priests to persecute Jeremiah.

How deeply hardened people become when they imagine their possession of power gives them the right to do harm!

The exiles were already in terrible bondage because of their contempt toward God's messengers.

Yet under that discipline, some continued sinning even more.

Suffering alone does not cure sin. The Lord's grace must work with correction if it is to renew a heart.

Those who reject the blessing of God's word, as Shemaiah did, deserve to lose its benefit.

Many charges raised against active Christians in every age amount to little more than this:

They urge people to attend to their true interests and duties, and to wait for God's promises in his appointed way.

The zealous servant of the Lord will use every means to profit those who are far off, as well as those who are near him. The art of writing is very profitable for this end; and by the art of printing it is rendered most beneficial for circulating the knowledge of the word of God. If they live in the fear of God, they may live comfortably in Babylon. In all conditions of life, it is our wisdom and duty not to throw away the comfort of what we may have, because we have not all we would have. They are directed to seek the good of the country where they were captives. While the king of Babylon protected them, they must live quiet and peaceable lives under him, in all godliness and honesty; patiently leaving it to God to work deliverance for them in due time.
[Jer.29.8-Jer.29.19]
Verses 8-19 Let men beware how they call those prophets whom they choose after their own fancies, and how they consider their fancies and dreams to be revelations from God. False prophets flatter people in their sins, because they love to be flattered; and they speak smoothly to their prophets, that their prophets may speak smoothly to them. God promises that they should return after seventy years were accomplished. By this it appears, that the seventy years of the captivity are not to be reckoned from the last captivity, but the first. It will be the bringing to pass of God's good word to them. This shall form God's purposes. We often do not know our own minds, but the Lord is never at an uncertainty. We are sometimes ready to fear that God's designs are all against us; but as to his own people, even that which seems evil, is for good. He will give them, not the expectations of their fears, or the expectations of their fancies, but the expectations of their faith; the end he has promised, which will be the best for them. When the Lord pours out an especial spirit of prayer, it is a good sign that he is coming toward us in mercy. Promises are given to quicken and encourage prayer. He never said, Seek ye me in vain. Those who remained at Jerusalem would be utterly destroyed, notwithstanding what the false prophets said to the contrary. The reason has often been given, and it justifies the eternal ruin of impenitent sinners; Because they have not hearkened to my words; I called, but they refused.
[Jer.29.20-Jer.29.32]
Verses 20-32 Jeremiah foretells judgments upon the false prophets, who deceived the Jews in Babylon. Lying was bad; lying to the people of the Lord, to delude them into a false hope, was worse; but pretending to rest their own lies upon the God of truth, was worst of all. They flattered others in their sins, because they could not reprove them without condemning themselves. The most secret sins are known to God; and there is a day coming when he will bring to light all the hidden works of darkness. Shemaiah urges the priests to persecute Jeremiah. Their hearts are wretchedly hardened who justify doing mischief by having power to do it. They were in a miserable thraldom for mocking the messengers of the Lord, and misusing his prophets; yet in their distress they trespass still more against the Lord. Afflictions will not of themselves cure men of their sins, unless the grace of God works with them. Those who slight the blessings, deserve to lose the benefit of God's word, like Shemaiah. The accusations against many active Christians in all ages, amount to no more than this, that they earnestly counsel men to attend to their true interest and duties, and to wait for the performance of God's promises in his appointed way.
